concepts.name: Claude Agent SDK sessions: resume and fork

questions.prompt: A predicate is declared `def is_text(b: TextBlock | ToolUseBlock) -> TypeIs[TextBlock]`. In the `else` branch of `if is_text(block):`, what type does a type checker give `block`?

choices.text: `TextBlock | ToolUseBlock`, since only the `if` branch is ever narrowed
`ToolUseBlock`, because `TypeIs` narrows the `else` branch as well
`object`, because a predicate that fails erases what was known before
`Never`, since the predicate claims every input is a `TextBlock`

questions.explanation: When a `TypeIs` predicate returns `False`, the argument is narrowed to exclude the named type, so only `ToolUseBlock` is left. Narrowing only in the `if` branch is how `TypeGuard` behaves. Neither checks the function body at runtime: the predicate must really return what it claims.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints
sources.claim: With TypeIs, a True return narrows the argument to the intersection of its type and the narrowed type, and a False return narrows it to exclude that type; with TypeGuard, a False return leaves the type unchanged.

questions.prompt: A job adds `permissions: { pull-requests: write }` so one of its steps can comment on the pull request. What access does that job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` now have to the repository's contents?

choices.text: Read, because `contents: read` is always kept as a baseline
The repository's default, since one entry only adds access
None, because every permission you don't list is set to `none`
Write, because `pull-requests: write` implies `contents: write`

questions.explanation: Once you specify any permission in `permissions`, every one you didn't list is set to `none`. So a job that also runs `actions/checkout` needs `contents: read` listed too. The rule makes least privilege the default: you grant exactly what each job needs.

sources.title: Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions
sources.claim: The `permissions` key modifies the default permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN at workflow or job level; if you specify the access for any permission, all of those not specified are set to none.

questions.prompt: A Claude Agent SDK service analyses a repository in one `query()` call, and users later ask follow-ups, sometimes wanting to try another approach without losing the first. How would you use sessions for this, and what does a session not restore?

model_answer.summary: Capture the session ID from the result, `resume` it for follow-ups and `resume` with `fork_session` for alternatives; a session restores the conversation, not the files, and its transcript is local to the machine.
key_points: Capture `session_id` from the result message and pass it as `resume` to continue with the full prior context
Fork with `resume` plus `fork_session=True`: the fork gets a new session ID and a copy of the history, and the original is unchanged
Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem: file edits made in a fork are real for every session in that directory (use file checkpointing to revert them)
Session files are stored locally under `~/.claude/projects/`, so resuming on another host needs a session store or the moved file

questions.explanation: Resuming saves the agent from re-reading files and re-doing analysis, and forking lets you branch without spoiling the original thread. The tempting assumption is that a fork is a sandbox: it only branches the history, so its edits land on disk for everyone.

sources.title: Work with sessions
sources.claim: The session ID is on every result message; `resume` returns to a session with full context; `fork_session` creates a new session with a copy of the history and leaves the original unchanged; sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem; session files are local to the machine that created them.

questions.prompt: You write `def is_str_list(val: list[object]) -> TypeGuard[list[str]]`. Why is `TypeGuard`, not `TypeIs`, the right choice here?

choices.text: `TypeIs` only works when its body is a single `isinstance` check
`TypeGuard` checks each element at runtime, and `TypeIs` doesn't
`TypeIs` can only narrow a union, and `list[object]` is not a union
`TypeIs` needs a type consistent with the input; `list[str]` isn't

questions.explanation: The type inside `TypeIs` must be consistent with the argument's type, and `list[str]` is not a subtype of `list[object]` (lists are invariant). `TypeGuard` has no such rule and narrows to exactly the named type in the `if` branch, which is what the docs' `is_str_list` example uses. Neither construct checks anything at runtime.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints
sources.claim: The type inside TypeIs must be consistent with the type of the function's argument; TypeGuard narrows to exactly its type in the True branch, as in the `is_str_list(val: list[object]) -> TypeGuard[list[str]]` example.

questions.prompt: Your repository's workflows lint and test on every push, and one job publishes a release. How would you set the `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions, and how does the `permissions` key behave at workflow and job level?

model_answer.summary: Set a read-only default for the workflow and raise permissions only in the release job; the job-level key overrides the workflow's, and any permission not listed becomes `none`.
key_points: Grant the least access: a workflow-level default of `contents: read` for lint and test
Give only the release job the extra permission it needs, such as `contents: write`, with a job-level `permissions` key
A job-level `permissions` overrides the workflow-level one, and listing any permission sets every unlisted one to `none`
`permissions: {}` disables all permissions for jobs that need no token access

questions.explanation: GitHub recommends a read-only default for repository contents and raising permissions per job, so a compromised lint step can't push code. The rule that unlisted permissions become `none` is what catches people out: listing one write permission can silently remove the read access checkout needs.

sources.title: Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions
sources.claim: `permissions` can be set for a workflow or a job, the job value overriding the workflow's; specifying any permission sets all unspecified ones to none; `permissions: {}` disables all.

sources.title: Secure use reference
sources.claim: It's good security practice to set the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission to read access only for repository contents, and increase permissions as required for individual jobs.

questions.prompt: You resume a Claude Agent SDK session with `fork_session=True`, and the forked agent edits `auth.py` in the same working directory. What happens to the original session?

choices.text: Nothing at all: a fork works on its own private copy of the files
Its history is unchanged, but the `auth.py` edit is real for it
Its history gains the fork's turns as soon as the fork's run ends
It is closed, and only the fork's new session ID can be resumed

questions.explanation: A fork gets its own session ID and a copy of the history, and the original's history stays as it was, so both can be resumed. But forking branches the conversation, not the filesystem: the edit is on disk for any session in that directory. To revert file changes, the docs point to file checkpointing.

sources.title: Work with sessions
sources.claim: Forking creates a new session with its own ID and a copy of the history while the original stays unchanged; it branches the conversation history, not the filesystem, so a forked agent's file edits are real and visible to any session in the same directory.

questions.prompt: A Claude Agent SDK service analyses a repository in one `query()` call, and users later ask follow-ups, sometimes wanting to try another approach without losing the first. Which statements about sessions are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Read `session_id` from the result message and pass it as `resume` to keep full context
`resume` with `fork_session=True` gives a new session ID and leaves the original as is
A fork also snapshots the files, so its file edits stay hidden from the original session
Sessions are stored in Anthropic's cloud, so any host can resume one using only its ID
Session files are local to the machine; another host needs a session store or the file

questions.explanation: The session ID is on every result message, and passing it as `resume` returns to that session with its full context. Forking (`resume` plus `fork_session=True`) creates a new session with its own ID and a copy of the history, leaving the original unchanged. Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem: a fork's file edits are real for every session in that directory (use file checkpointing to revert them). Session files are written locally, so resuming on another host needs a session store adapter or the moved file.

sources.title: Work with sessions
sources.claim: The `session_id` is on every result message; `resume` returns to that session with full context; forking creates a new session with its own ID and a copy of the history while the original stays unchanged; sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem, so a fork's file edits are real for any session in the same directory; session files are local to the machine that created them, so another host needs a session store or the moved session file.

questions.prompt: Your repository's workflow lints and tests on every push, and one job publishes a release. Which statements about the `GITHUB_TOKEN` `permissions` key are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A job-level `permissions` key overrides the workflow-level one for that job
Listing any one permission leaves every unlisted one at its default access
Default to `contents: read`, and give only the release job `contents: write`
`permissions: {}` disables every permission, for jobs that need no token
A job can only narrow the workflow's permissions, so the release job can't write

questions.explanation: `permissions` can be set for the whole workflow or per job, and a job's own key applies to that job. GitHub's advice is least privilege: read-only `contents` by default, raised only for the jobs that need it, such as the release job. Specifying any permission sets all the unspecified ones to `none`, not to their defaults, and `permissions: {}` turns them all off.

sources.title: Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions
sources.claim: `permissions` can be a top-level key for all jobs or set within a specific job, which then gets the access rights it specifies; if you specify access for any permission, all unspecified ones are set to `none`; `permissions: {}` disables all permissions.

sources.title: Secure use reference
sources.claim: Set the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission to read access only for repository contents, then increase permissions as required for individual jobs in the workflow file.
